strengths: Addresses an appealing and practical problem: incorporating controllable, dynamic global weather effects (snowfall, rainfall, fog, sandstorms) and falling objects into reconstructed static 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes.

The hybrid MPM-Gaussian framework effectively leverages continuum mechanics for physically plausible trajectory and orientation simulation, coupled with an active-particle pruning strategy to maintain computational efficiency.

The specialized collision handling techniques (such as normal-aligned surface projection for accumulation and volumetric wetness diffusion for rain) produce visually convincing dynamic-static boundary interactions.
The paper is well-written, clearly organized, and provides extensive implementation parameters and hyperparameter configurations in the appendix for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is relatively modest: the pipeline primarily integrates existing components (TSDF mesh extraction from 2DGS, MPM continuum simulation via Taichi/PhysGaussian/Feature Splatting, and 3DGS rendering) augmented by standard heuristic computer graphics rules for surface projection and dampness.

The quantitative evaluation is limited: because comparisons are drawn against static editing methods (ClimateNeRF and GaussCtrl), the evaluation relies entirely on 2D image-text alignment metrics (CLIPSim, CLIPDir, VQAScore). There are no quantitative evaluations or user studies assessing physical plausibility, temporal consistency, or dynamic realism.

Lack of physically based optical and illumination interaction: weather phenomena significantly alter environmental lighting (e.g., specular reflections on wet surfaces, diffuse scattering in fog, refracted rain streaks). The method relies on simple color darkening and opacity blending without true relighting or material-aware specular response.

Interaction is strictly unidirectional: dynamic particles interact with static scene boundaries as rigid obstacles, but the static scene elements cannot react, deform, or blow in the wind (e.g., foliage or branches swaying during storms).

strengths: Addresses an appealing and practical problem: incorporating interactive, dynamic global weather phenomena (snow, rain, sandstorm, fog) and falling objects into static 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes.

The combination of MPM-based simulation with active particle tracking and specialized mesh-based collision handling (surface projection for snow/sand, volumetric wetness grid for rain) yields visually plausible interaction effects.
Demonstrates good versatility across diverse weather types and object dynamics (e.g., leaves, feathers, drones), with user controllability over particle quantity, velocity, and visual properties.
The paper is clearly written, easy to follow, and provides detailed simulation/rendering parameters in the appendix to aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual and technical novelty is somewhat limited: the method largely combines existing tools—TSDF mesh extraction from 3DGS, off-the-shelf MPM simulation in Taichi (following Feature Splatting / PhysGaussian), hand-tuned Gaussian appearance parameters, and geometric snapping heuristics for accumulation.

Evaluation against baselines is problematic: comparing a dynamic simulation pipeline against static editing methods (ClimateNeRF, GaussCtrl) using static image metrics (CLIP Similarity, CLIP Direction, VQAScore) does not evaluate temporal consistency, motion plausibility, or physical fidelity. A structured user study evaluating motion realism and physical plausibility would provide much stronger evidence.

Collision and interaction modeling is strictly one-way and largely heuristic: the static scene geometry cannot deform or react (e.g., wind bending foliage, accumulating snow weighing down branches), and accumulation/wetness effects rely on heuristic post-processing rather than full physical phase transitions or fluid accumulation.

Visual assessment of dynamic phenomena (especially rainfall and fine particulates) is difficult to judge reliably from static paper figures alone, making thorough video-based perceptual evaluations critical.

strengths: Compelling and practical objective: Adding physically plausible global dynamic weather effects (snow, rain, sandstorm, fog) and falling objects into reconstructed static 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes is a useful application for graphics and virtual content creation.

Broad demonstration of different phenomena: The paper demonstrates the pipeline across several distinct weather conditions as well as dynamic rigid/falling objects (leaves, feathers, drones), showing the versatility of the overall workflow.

Clear implementation recipe: The appendix provides extensive and reproducible parameter settings for the Material Point Method (MPM) simulations (Young's modulus, Poisson ratio, emission rates) and rendering attributes across each effect.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The pipeline is primarily an engineering combination of established techniques—TSDF mesh extraction from 3DGS, off-the-shelf MPM particle simulation via Taichi (following PhysGaussian and Feature Splatting), and binding pre-generated text-to-3D Gaussians (GaussianDreamer) or manual primitives to particle trajectories. The collision handling relies on simple geometric heuristics (nearest-point projection onto an Open3D mesh surface and a heuristic 3D wetness grid) rather than novel physical or neural formulations.

Mismatched and unconvincing quantitative evaluation: The quantitative benchmarks (Table 1) evaluate CLIP similarity, CLIP direction, and VQAScore against static 3D scene editing methods (ClimateNeRF and GaussCtrl). Comparing a dynamic particle simulation framework against static 2D-diffusion-based appearance editors on text-image alignment metrics does not effectively measure physical plausibility, dynamic realism, temporal coherence, or contact accuracy.

Lack of temporal and physical evaluation metrics: For a submission fundamentally centered on dynamic animation, there are no evaluations of motion plausibility, physical consistency (e.g., terminal velocities, drag forces, flow dynamics), temporal flicker/popping, or user studies assessing whether users perceive the motion and accumulation as realistic compared to baseline graphics particle systems.

Heuristic simulation-geometry disconnect: Because MPM is run on a coarse $64^3$ grid, it cannot capture fine contacts directly, requiring ad-hoc post-processing (snapping particles along surface normals, artificial wetness grids). Furthermore, interactions remain strictly unidirectional (no foliage sway in wind/sandstorms, no structural deformability, and snow accumulation does not deform plastically under true MPM mechanics).
